en: *The Treatise on Arousing the Mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the Yoga of Vajraśekhara*, also titled *The General Explanation of Yoga:
The Exposition of the Meaning of the Practice of Bodhicitta Contemplation Spoken by the Śrāvaka School*.
Grand Master of the Household, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daixingshan Monastery—Grand Master of Great Universal Wisdom (Daguangzhi Ajari), Duke of Sushan with a fief of three thousand households, invested with purple robes, posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works, and bestowed the posthumous name Dajian (Great Mirror)—by Imperial Decree. The Grand Master of Great Universal Wisdom said:

"If there are those of superior faculties and superior wisdom who do not delight in the teachings of the non-Buddhists or the Two Vehicles, who possess great capacity for judgment, are courageous and resolute, and are free from doubt, they should cultivate the Buddha Vehicle."
One should give rise to this thought:
"I now aspire to seek Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and do not seek any other fruit.

Because of the firm resolve of this vow, the palaces of Māra tremble; all the Buddhas of the ten directions bear witness to it, and one shall constantly experience supreme bliss among gods and humans, remembering and never forgetting it in whatever place one is born.
If one aspires to attain the bodies of the various bodhisattvas within the yoga, this is also called "generating the bodhicitta.
Why? Because these venerable ones are all identical in essence to the body of the Great Vairocana Buddha.
Just as one who craves the title of official gives rise to the mind that seeks such an office and practices the conduct required for that office;
so too, one who craves wealth and treasures gives rise to the mind that seeks them and engages in the activities of managing and acquiring material goods.
Generally, when people seek either good or evil, they first manifest their intention and subsequently fulfill their resolve.
Thus, those who seek Bodhi give rise to the Bodhicitta and cultivate the practices of Bodhi.
Having already generated such a mind, one must understand the characteristics of the bodhicitta.
As for these characteristics, they are distinguished by way of three gates.

When the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were formerly on the causal ground, having generated this mind, they took ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the practice of vows (*praṇidhāna*), and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as their ethical discipline; until they attained Buddhahood, they never forgot them for even a moment.
Because it is only within the Mantra Dharma that one attains Buddhahood in this very body, it is for this reason that *samādhi* is taught; it is omitted and not mentioned in other teachings.
These are: first, practice and vows; second, ultimate truth; and third, *samādhi*.
Regarding the initial vow: it means that a person who practices should constantly maintain such a mind:
"I shall bring benefit and peace to the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, regarding all conscious beings of the ten directions as my own self."

What is called "benefit" refers to exhorting and inspiring all sentient beings, causing them all to dwell securely in unsurpassed bodhi, and never allowing them to attain liberation through the teachings of the two vehicles.

The practitioner of mantras knows that all sentient beings contain the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha and are all capable of abiding in unsurpassed bodhi; therefore, they do not cause them to attain liberation through the teachings of the two vehicles.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachments that they do not realize it."
If one is free from deluded thoughts, then all-knowing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhūjñāna*), and unimpeded wisdom (*asanga-jñāna*) will manifest before one.
What is called "peaceful bliss" means that the practitioner realizes that all sentient beings will ultimately achieve Buddhahood; therefore, they do not dare to treat them with contempt.

Furthermore, within the gateway of great compassion, one should especially strive to provide rescue; whatever the sentient beings seek, one should grant and bestow it upon them, even at the cost of one's own body and life, never begrudging that life, so that their lives may be preserved and they may be made joyful.
Once they have drawn near, they place their trust in the words of the teacher; because of this intimacy, they may then be instructed.
Sentient beings are ignorant and deluded, making them difficult to lead across; thus, the practitioner of *mantra* employs skillful means to guide them forward.
Regarding the second, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): it is the contemplation that all phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Why do they lack intrinsic nature?

It is because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are attached to fame, profit, and the requisites for livelihood, striving only to secure their own physical well-being, and thus unrestrainedly indulge in the three poisons and the five desires.
Mantra practitioners should truly feel weary of [this world] and should indeed renounce it.

Furthermore, various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to their bodies and lives; some seek to attain longevity by dwelling in the celestial palaces of the immortals through the aid of medicinal herbs, while others take rebirth in the heavens as their ultimate goal.

The practitioner of mantras should observe that even when their karmic forces are exhausted, as long as they have not yet abandoned the afflictions of the triple world, their past calamities remain unextinguished and evil thoughts continue to arise.
In future times, they will sink into the ocean of suffering from which it is difficult to escape.
You should know that the teachings of the non-Buddhists are likewise like illusions, dreams, and mirages.
Furthermore, among those of the two vehicles, Śrāvakas cling to the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, while Pratyekabuddhas cling to the twelve links of dependent origination.

Knowing that the four great elements and the five aggregates are ultimately subject to decay and extinction, he gives rise to a profound sense of weary detachment; shattering the attachments of sentient beings, he diligently cultivates the fundamental Dharma to realize its fruit, proceeding toward Great Nirvana as his ultimate goal.

A practitioner of mantra should observe that although those of the Two Vehicles have destroyed the attachment to a personal self, they still possess attachment to phenomena; they merely quiet the mental consciousness and know nothing else.

Furthermore, having attained the stage of fruition, they have already reduced their bodies to ashes and extinguished their wisdom to enter nirvana; like the great void, they are profoundly and eternally quiescent. For those of fixed nature, it is difficult for [the Buddha-nature] to arise; it must wait until the limits of the kalpa are fulfilled before it can finally manifest.
If one is of indeterminate nature, regardless of the limit of kalpas, upon encountering the right conditions, they will turn their mind toward the Mahāyāna and arise from the "City of Transformation.

Because they have already transcended the three realms and possessed faith in the Buddha from the past, they receive the skillful means of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and thereby resolve to attain the Great Mind. Starting from the initial stage of the ten levels of faith, they traverse all subsequent stages, undergoing difficult practices and asceticism throughout three incalculable kalpas, until finally attaining Buddhahood.
Having understood that the wisdom of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is narrow and inferior, it is not to be sought after.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who give rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, training universally in all dharma-gates without exception. After passing through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they fully complete the cultivation of the six pāramitās and the myriad practices; yet, the realization of the fruit of Buddhahood is achieved only after a long duration. This is because the dharmas they have practiced are dispersed, resulting in a sequential progression.

Now, when a practitioner of mantras has completed the aforementioned visualization, they further generate a mind intent on benefiting and bringing peace to all sentient beings throughout the entire realm of beings without exception. Through the certainty of great compassion, they forever transcend the realms of non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles; furthermore, by practicing the supreme yoga-dharma, they are able to enter the rank of Buddhahood from the state of an ordinary being, thereby transcending even the realms of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
Furthermore, one deeply understands that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why do they lack intrinsic nature?
This has already been explained in detail above.

Now, the dharmas of the deluded path arise from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which further develops into immeasurable and boundless afflictions (*kleśa*) such that beings transmigrate through the six realms.
Once awakening is attained, false conceptualization ceases and is eliminated, and all various phenomena (*dharma*) are extinguished; therefore, they possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, the Buddhas, out of their great compassion, manifest activity from the ultimate truth to rescue and gather in sentient beings. They provide various Dharma gates as medicine according to the illness, applying remedies that correspond to each specific affliction. When those lost at the ford encounter a raft and reach the other shore, they must also abandon the Dharma, for it lacks intrinsic nature.
As stated in the *Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*:
"All phenomena are signless, which is to say they have the characteristic of space; having cultivated this contemplation, it is called the ultimate bodhicitta."
One should know that all phenomena are empty.

Having realized that phenomena are fundamentally unborn, the essence of the mind remains as it is; seeing neither body nor mind, one abides in the wisdom of ultimate reality—quiescent, equanimous, and perfect—and ensures that this state is never lost.
If deluded thoughts arise, recognize them and do not follow after them.
When delusions cease, the source of the mind is empty and still; all virtues are fully present, and its wondrous function is inexhaustible.
Therefore, the Buddhas of the ten directions take ultimate truth and the practice of vows as their precepts.
Those who possess this mind alone are able to turn the wheel of Dharma, benefiting both themselves and others.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"Compassionate light and wisdom as the sovereign, / Skillful means acting in mutual accord,
/ With a mind of pure faith and understanding, / Such is the Tathāgata’s immeasurable power."
Unobstructed wisdom manifests before them; self-awakened and not dependent on another, they possess all that is equal to the Tathāgata, having given rise to this most supreme mind.
As soon as the Son of the Buddha first gives rise to such a wondrous jewel-like mind, it is said:
Thus one transcends the stage of ordinary beings and enters the sphere of the Buddhas' practice.
Born into the family of the Tathāgatas, one’s lineage is free from blemish;
equal to the Buddhas, one is certain to achieve unsurpassed awakening.
"As soon as such a mind arises, one immediately enters the first stage (bhūmi);
the mind’s joy is immovable, like the King of Mountains.
Furthermore, according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
From the first stage through to the tenth stage, throughout each stage, great compassion is paramount.
As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa* states:
"The Buddha-mind is none other than great compassion."
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Homage to Cunda! Although his body is that of a human, his mind is identical to the Buddha-mind.
It also says:
"Great King of Physicians who has compassion for the world, Whose body and wisdom are both utterly tranquil;
In the dharma of non-self, there is the true self— Therefore, I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One."
There is no distinction between the initial resolve and the ultimate goal; yet of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult.
To seek to deliver others before one has delivered oneself—therefore, I pay homage to the initial resolve.
Having resolved their minds, they become teachers of humans and devas, surpassing both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
such a resolve transcends the three realms, and for this reason it is called the most unsurpassed.
As stated in the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*:
"Awakening is the cause, great compassion is the root, and skillful means are the culmination.
Regarding the third point, samādhi: once the practitioner of mantras has contemplated in this way, how can they realize unsurpassed awakening?
One should know that it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that one must abide in the great bodhicitta of Samantabhadra;
for all sentient beings inherently possess the *sattva* [nature], yet they are bound by the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
The great compassion of all Buddhas, through skillful wisdom, teaches this profound and secret yoga, causing practitioners to visualize a white moon disc within their own minds.

By performing this contemplation, one clearly perceives that the fundamental mind is profoundly still and pure, like the light of the full moon pervading the void without any discrimination. It is also called "awakened realization," also called the "Pure Dharma-realm," and also called the "Ocean of the Prajñāpāramitā of True Reality. It can contain all manner of immeasurable treasures and samādhis, just as the full moon is immaculate and distinct.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings universally contain the mind of Samantabhadra, I perceive my own mind as being shaped like a lunar disc.
For what reason is the lunar disc used as a metaphor?
That is to say, the essence of the full moon, perfectly bright and complete, is analogous to the bodhicitta.
Generally, the lunar disc has sixteen phases, which metaphorically represent the sixteen great bodhisattvas from Vajrasattva to Vajramuṣṭi within the yoga system.
Among the thirty-seven honored ones, each of the five directional Buddhas represents a specific wisdom.
Akṣobhya Buddha of the east, through his causal realization, becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, also known as Vajra Wisdom.
In the south is Ratnasambhava Buddha; because he has perfected the wisdom of equality, he is also called the Wisdom of Consecration.
In the west is Amitābha Buddha; because he has perfected the wisdom of wondrous observation, he is also called the Lotus Wisdom, or the Wisdom of Turning the Wheel of Dharma.
In the north is Amoghasiddhi Buddha; because he has perfected the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is To Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), he is also called the Wisdom of Action (*karma-jñāna*).
In the center is Vairocana Buddha; because he has perfected the Wisdom of the Dharma Realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*), it serves as his fundamental basis.
From the above four Buddha-wisdoms, the four Bodhisattvas of the Pāramitās are born.
These four Bodhisattvas—namely, Vajra, Ratna, Dharma, and Karma—are the mothers who generate, sustain, and nourish all the sages and worthies of the three periods of time.
Thereupon, the seals were completed, and from within the essential nature of the *dharmadhātu*, the four Buddhas emerged.
Each Tathāgata of the four directions presides over four Bodhisattvas.
To the east, Akṣobhya Buddha presides over four Bodhisattvas: Vajrasattva, Vajrarāja, Vajrarāga, and Sujaya as the four Bodhisattvas.
In the south, Ratnasambhava Buddha encompasses four bodhisattvas; Vajraratna, Vajraprabha, Vajraketu, and Vajrahāsa constitute these four bodhisattvas.
In the western direction, Amitābha Buddha gathers four bodhisattvas: Vajradharma, Vajratīkṣṇa, Vajrakāra, and Vajrabhāṣa constitute these four bodhisattvas.
In the north, Buddha Amoghasiddhi encompasses four bodhisattvas: Vajrakarma, Vajrarakṣa, Vajradaṃṣṭra, and Vajramuṣṭi are these four bodhisattvas.
Each of the Buddhas of the four directions is accompanied by four bodhisattvas, constituting the sixteen great bodhisattvas.

Among the thirty-seven honored ones, excluding the five Buddhas, the four pāramitās, the latter four modes of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), and the eight offerings, one takes only these sixteen great bodhisattvas as being subsumed under the Buddhas of the four directions.

Furthermore, within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), there are likewise sixteen meanings.

All sentient beings possess within the substance of their minds a portion of pure nature (*viśuddha-dhātu*) in which all practices are fully present; its essence is extremely subtle, radiant, and luminous, remaining unchanged even as they transmigrate through the six realms of existence, like one-sixteenth of the moon.
Generally, when the first phase of the moon’s appearance coincides with the moment of conjunction, it does not manifest because its luminous nature is eclipsed by the light of the sun.
Subsequently, as the new moon begins to arise, it increases day by day until, on the fifteenth day, it becomes perfectly full and unobstructed.
Therefore, the practitioner first causes the letter A to arise clearly within the fundamental mind; then, gradually making it pure and distinct, they realize the wisdom of non-arising.
Now, as for the syllable *a*, it signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen (*anutpāda*).
According to the commentary on the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*, the syllable *a* possesses five meanings:

first, the short sound of *a* is the bodhicitta; second, the drawn-out sound of *a* is the practice of bodhi; third, the long sound of *ā* is the meaning of realizing bodhi; fourth, the short sound of *aḥ* is the meaning of parinirvāṇa; and fifth, the drawn-out sound of *aḥ* is the meaning of being fully endowed with the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).

Furthermore, the letter *A* is also correlated with and explained in relation to the four characters—opening (*kai*), showing (*shi*), awakening (*go*), and entering (*nyu*)—found within the *Lotus Sūtra*.
"Opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" simultaneously opens both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, just like the initial letter *A*, which carries the meaning of the *bodhicitta*.
The character "Shi" (示) signifies the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; like the second letter, A, it carries the meaning of the practice of bodhi.
The character "Wu" (悟) signifies awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; like the third letter, Am, it carries the meaning of realizing bodhi.
As for the character "entering" (ru), it means entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is like the fourth "evil" character (*aku*), which signifies the meaning of *parinirvāṇa*.
To summarize, these are fully accomplished; the fifth "evil" character signifies the perfection of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyajñāna*).
He then praised the syllable A as having the meaning of the bodhicitta.
The verse says:
“Upon a white eight-petaled lotus at the gate of one cubit, The syllable A appears brilliantly with a pale white radiance.”
"Place both meditative concentration and wisdom into the vajra-bind, and summon the Tathāgata’s tranquil wisdom.
Regarding the support for the letter A: examine it with precise and certain observation; one should contemplate the perfectly luminous pure consciousness.
If one perceives it for even a moment, this is called seeing the true ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
If one perceives it constantly, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva.

If it further increases and develops, becoming vast and pervasive throughout the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), equal in measure to empty space, and free in its contraction and expansion, one shall possess all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*).
All practitioners who cultivate the yoga of contemplation must fully practice the three secret activities to realize the meaning of the five stages of bodily perfection (*pañcakrama*).
Regarding these three secrets: first, the secret of body refers to such acts as forming ritual mudrās to summon the assembly of noble beings.
Second, the secret of speech (*vāgguhya*) refers to the clear and distinct recitation of mantra syllables without error.
Third, the secret of mind (*manoguhyaka*) refers to abiding in the yoga of the corresponding visualization of the pure, full moon, contemplating the bodhicitta.

Next, to clarify the formation of the body through the five stages: first is the penetrating mind; second is the bodhicitta; third is the vajra-mind; fourth is the vajra-body; and fifth is the realization of unsurpassed bodhi and the attainment of the adamantine, solid body.
However, it is only when these five characteristics are fully present that the body of the Honored One is perfected.

This perfect luminosity is the body of Samantabhadra and is also the mind of Samantabhadra; it is identical to that of all Buddhas of the ten directions. Furthermore, while there may be a sequence of before and after regarding the cultivation and realization throughout the three periods of time, upon reaching awakening, there is no past, future, or present.
The minds of ordinary beings are like closed lotus flowers, while the Buddha-mind is like the full moon.

If this contemplation is perfected, then the lands of the ten directions—whether pure or impure—the sentient beings of the six realms, the stages and ranks of the practices of the three vehicles, the formation and destruction of the lands throughout the three periods of time, the distinctions among the karmas of sentient beings, the characteristics of the practices on the causal grounds of Bodhisattvas, and all the Buddhas of the three periods of time will all appear therein. One realizes the body of the Honored One and fulfills all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
The *Mahāvairocana Sūtra* states:
"Such is the true mind; therefore, it has been proclaimed by the Buddha.
Question:
It is said that those of the two vehicles cannot attain Buddhahood because they possess attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Now, regarding the instruction to cultivate the *samādhi* of the bodhicitta, how does this differ [from their practice]?
Answer:

Because those of the Two Vehicles possess attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), they realize the principle after a long time and become submerged in emptiness and stalled in quiescence; thus, they must wait for a limited number of eons before they can give rise to the Great Mind.
Furthermore, within the gate of scattered goodness, they pass through incalculable eons; therefore, these states are sufficient grounds for weary detachment and are not to be relied upon.

Now, although a practitioner of mantras has already shattered the two attachments to persons and phenomena and possesses the wisdom of correct vision into reality, they may still be unable to realize the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom due to the obstructions of beginningless time.

For those who seek the wondrous Way and practice the successive stages from the level of an ordinary being to the rank of a Buddha, this very samādhi enables them to penetrate the self-nature of all Buddhas, awaken to the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas, and realize the wisdom of the essential nature of the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, they achieve the self-nature body (*svabhāvakāya*), enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and flow-on body (*nisyandakāya*) of the Great Vairocana Buddha.
Because the body of natural outflow (*niṣyanda-kāya*) has not yet been realized by the practitioner, it is logically necessary to cultivate it.
Thus, the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra* states:
"Siddhi arises from the mind."
As stated in the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-tantra*:

"The Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddhi first sat upon the Vajrāsana and realized the Unsurpassed Way; he was then granted this 'Mind-Ground' (*cittabhūmi*) by all the Buddhas, whereby he was able to realize the fruit."

If people of the present day resolve their minds and practice according to the instructions, without rising from their seats, samādhi will manifest before them, and they shall thereby achieve the body of the tutelary deity.
Therefore, the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra* states in the "Method of the Sequence of Offerings":
"If one lacks the power to extensively increase and abide in the Dharma, one should simply contemplate the bodhicitta."
The Buddha taught that herein all the myriad practices are complete, gradually fulfilling the pure and immaculate dharmas.
This bodhicitta is able to encompass and contain all the meritorious dharmas of all Buddhas.
If cultivation and realization manifest, one becomes a teacher of all;
if one returns to the source, it is the Land of Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha), where one can accomplish all tasks without rising from one's seat.
In praise of the bodhicitta:
If a person seeks the wisdom of the Buddha And penetrates the bodhicitta,
The body born of parents will swiftly Realize the state of Great Enlightenment.
A Treatise on Arousing the Mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara, in one fascicle.
